Narrative: Spiny mice (Acomys) are the only mammals known to regenerate full-thickness skin — including hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and arrector pili muscles — without scarring. When threatened by a predator, they shed large patches of skin (autotomy) and regrow it completely, something no lab mouse can do. The regeneration extends beyond skin: Acomys can regenerate ear hole punches (including cartilage), kidney tissue after ischemia-reperfusion injury, and spinal cord tissue after injury — all with minimal fibrosis compared to Mus musculus. Gusev's group at Kazan Federal University (Filatov 2024) revealed a distinctive hemostasis phenotype: spiny mouse blood forms stronger hemostatic seals with elevated clottable fibrinogen, denser fibrin-rich clots, and superior plasma clot stiffness. This robust hemostasis may be an adaptation that enables the risky strategy of shedding skin — you need reliable clotting before you can afford to lose tissue. The molecular drivers are still being mapped: Acomys wounds show reduced TGF-beta signaling, a macrophage response biased toward pro-regenerative rather than pro-fibrotic polarization, and Wnt pathway activity resembling embryonic patterning rather than adult scarring. No single gene has been identified as the master switch — this appears to be a systems-level rewiring of the wound response. The challenge for translational work is moving from descriptive -omics to causal gene targets.
Short Description: Skin punched clean through heals back whole—hair follicles, glands, and cartilage regrow instead of scarring, driven by low TGF-beta signaling and clot-forming blood 2-3x stronger than a lab mouse's. A 4mm ear hole closes in about 60 days with full structure restored, versus permanent scarring in Mus. This exists only in the Cairo spiny mouse—no transgenic transfer into mice attempted. No master gene runs it: TGF-beta, macrophage signaling, and Wnt patterning would need rewiring together.
Mechanism: Systems-level wound response: reduced TGF-beta/fibrotic signaling; pro-regenerative (M2-like) macrophage polarization; Wnt pathway activity resembling embryonic patterning; distinctive hemostasis with elevated fibrinogen and denser fibrin-rich clots (Filatov 2024). Regeneration includes hair follicles, sebaceous glands, cartilage, and potentially kidney and spinal cord tissue.
Achievements (effect sizes): Seifert 2012 Nature: Acomys regenerated 4mm ear punches with cartilage, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands in ~60 days (Mus scarred). Brant 2015: full-thickness dorsal skin wounds healed without fibrosis. Filatov 2024 IJMS: Acomys blood formed 2-3× stronger fibrin clots vs Balb/c mice. Simkin 2017: kidney ischemia-reperfusion — Acomys showed reduced fibrosis and preserved nephron architecture. Matias Santos 2023: ear regeneration involves blastema-like structure with Wnt/beta-catenin signaling.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (multiple mammalian organ systems) + T6 (replicated across independent labs)
Translational Gaps: No single master-switch gene identified; systems-level program likely requires multiple coordinated interventions; no transgenic experiments transferring Acomys wound program to Mus; no human-cell studies; hemostasis-regeneration link is correlative, not causally demonstrated.
Key References (DOIs): Seifert Nature 2012 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11499 | Filatov IJMS 2024 https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms252312867 | Brant Wound Repair Regen 2015 https://doi.org/10.1111/wrr.12319 | Simkin Nat Commun 2017 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-017-01671-5
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: NOT a single-gene candidate — included as a systems-level enhancement program. Translating Acomys regeneration may require rewiring TGF-beta signaling, macrophage polarization, and Wnt patterning simultaneously. Hemostasis connection (Filatov 2024) is from Gusev's lab but causal relationship between clotting phenotype and regeneration is unproven. Acomys are small rodents; whether the program scales to larger mammals is unknown. Some regenerative capacity (ear punch) may be shared with other Acomys species that differ in autotomy ability, suggesting the programs are separable.

Narrative: Arctic fish don't freeze because they're full of proteins that grab microscopic ice crystals the moment they form and glue themselves onto the crystal faces, stopping growth. The translational question is whether these molecules can do the same for mammalian tissue. The answer, so far, is a qualified yes. Adding 20 mg/mL of Type III antifreeze protein to standard mouse-ovary vitrification media raised intact follicle recovery from 28.9% to 44.7% — a big effect for cryobiology, where incremental gains are normal. AFPs have been used in clinical IVF oocyte freezing for years. Korkut Uygun's team at Harvard pushed the concept further, supercooling human donor livers to −4°C with AFPs and extending viable ex-vivo time by about 27 hours. The next step — actually transplanting a supercooled human liver — is imminent, not hypothetical. Chronic-exposure immunogenicity remains unresolved, and more AFP isn't always better: at high doses you can cause ice-needle damage.
Short Description: This protein grabs ice crystals the instant they form and clamps onto their faces, blocking growth so tissue survives freezing. In mouse ovary vitrification, 20 mg/mL raised intact follicle survival from 28.9% to 44.7%. It's already used in clinical IVF oocyte freezing, and a Harvard team supercooled a human liver to -4°C, adding about 27 hours of viable storage before transplant. Push the dose too high, though, and the protein forms damaging ice needles.
Mechanism: Non-colligative freezing-point depression via ice-face binding; thermal hysteresis; ice-recrystallization inhibition; membrane/ion-channel stabilization.
Achievements (effect sizes): Transgenic salmon (Hew 1991–99): stable Mendelian inheritance, seasonal AFP in serum but levels insufficient for seawater freeze-avoidance. Tobacco Type-I AFP (Kenward 1993): protein accumulated; Type-II AFP gave NO frost resistance despite 2% apoplast protein. Drosophila+beetle AFPs enhanced cold survival. Bagis 2006/2008: Type-III AFP-Tg mice, F7 germline; cryopreserved ovaries/testes retained function; live offspring after orthotopic ovary transplant. 20 mg/mL AFP in mouse ovary vitrification media: 44.7% intact follicle ratio vs 28.9% control (Lee 2015, PLoS ONE). Amir/Rubinsky 2004: AFPs in −1.3 °C 21-h rat heart preservation. AFPs in IVF oocyte vitrification (clinical-grade). Toner/Uygun/Tessier: supercooled human livers to −4 °C extended ex-vivo viability ~3× (+27 h); 2022–2024 partial-freezing 10-day rat liver storage at −10 to −15 °C.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (human ex-vivo organs, IVF cells) + T5 (Tg mice with functional tissue cryopreservation)
Translational Gaps: Supercooled human livers not yet transplanted; immunogenicity under chronic exposure.
Key References (DOIs): Bagis Mol Reprod Dev 2006 https://doi.org/10.1002/mrd.20566 | Lee PLoS ONE 2015 (AFP ovary cryo) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0126252 | de Vries Nat Biotechnol 2019 (supercooled liver) https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-019-0223-y
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Dose-response non-monotonic (ice-needle damage at higher concentration); Tg frost tolerance inconsistent. Kenward 1999 tobacco Type-II — no frost protection despite high expression. AquaBounty salmon uses growth hormone not AFP for phenotype.

Narrative: One woman in Colombia should have lost her mind by her forties. She carried PSEN1-E280A, a mutation that guarantees early-onset Alzheimer's in the world's largest autosomal dominant kindred — over 6,000 family members around Medellín. Instead, she remained cognitively intact until her seventies, three decades past the expected onset. The reason, reported by Arboleda-Velasquez in Nature Medicine in 2019, was two copies of an extraordinarily rare APOE variant called Christchurch (R136S). Her brain was loaded with amyloid but had remarkably little tau pathology and neurodegeneration. In 2018, Huang's group at Gladstone had already shown that converting APOE4 to APOE3 by CRISPR in human iPSC-derived neurons rescued tau phosphorylation, amyloid-beta overproduction, and GABAergic neuron loss. In 2023, Nelson and Huang engineered the R136S mutation into APOE4 mice and iPSC neurons and found that homozygous Christchurch edit rescued APOE4-driven tau pathology, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation. The idea of editing a patient's APOE4 alleles to a protective form is now the sharpest genetic target in Alzheimer's prevention. The catch: nobody has delivered a brain-wide APOE edit in a living animal, and APOE2 homozygosity itself raises cardiovascular lipid risk.
Short Description: This liver-made protein clears amyloid junk from between brain cells; the risky version slows cleanup, letting plaque pile up. A Colombian woman with a guaranteed early-onset mutation carried two rescue copies and stayed sharp into her seventies, thirty years past schedule. CRISPR-editing the risky version reverses tau damage in human neurons and mice, but nobody has edited a living brain. Two rescue copies also give 5-10% of people artery-clogging lipid disorder.
Mechanism: APOE: 299-aa secreted glycoprotein; E4 (Arg112/Arg158), E3 (Cys112/Arg158), E2 (Cys112/Cys158); Christchurch = R136S. E4 promotes Aβ aggregation, impairs Aβ clearance via LRP1/HSPG, increases tau phosphorylation. E2/Christchurch reduce HSPG binding, preserve microglial lipid homeostasis, diminish neuroinflammation.
Achievements (effect sizes): Wang 2018 Nat Med: iPSC APOE4/4 neurons showed increased p-tau, increased Aβ42/40, GABAergic neuron loss; CRISPR E4→E3 RESCUED all phenotypes. Nelson 2023 Nat Neurosci: APOE4-R136S homozygous in PS19 tauopathy mice rescued tau pathology, ~40% hippocampal volume loss prevented, neuroinflammation reduced. Arboleda-Velasquez 2019 Nat Med: PSEN1 carrier homozygous for APOE3-Christchurch — clinical onset delayed ~30 years.
Translational Gaps: No in-vivo brain-wide APOE editing in any animal; AAV/LNP BBB delivery; off-target base editing; APOE2/2 dysbetalipoproteinaemia risk (~5–10% of E2 homozygotes); mosaicism concerns.
Key References (DOIs): Wang Nat Med 2018 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-018-0004-z | Arboleda-Velasquez Nat Med 2019 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-019-0611-3 | Nelson Nat Neurosci 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-023-01480-8
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: APOE2 HOMOZYGOSITY carries its own risk: ~5–10% develop type III hyperlipoproteinaemia. Christchurch mutation is extraordinarily rare — single-case evidence. The Colombian woman had APOE3 background, not APOE4; whether R136S rescues E4 in humans is inferred from mice only. APOE4 effects are species-specific: E4 increased Aβ in human but NOT mouse neurons. Heterozygous R136S only partially protective.

Narrative: Aquaporins are tiny membrane pores that let water flow through cells about ten times faster than simple diffusion. Peter Agre won the 2003 Nobel for discovering them, after putting human AQP1 into frog eggs and watching them swell and burst. In mammals, knocking out AQP1 leaves mice producing dilute urine and losing weight when water is scarce — though the human version of this defect (Colton-null blood group) is essentially symptomless. The Australian water-holding frog survives months of drought in a cocoon, and is often cited as having a super-charged AQP1, but here's the awkward truth: the frog's actual AQP1 has never been cloned or tested in the lab. The entire chain — identify the special frog gene, transfer it to mammals, enhance hydration — is missing its first link. Even worse for the premise: in lungfish, AQP1 mRNA goes down during estivation, not up.
Short Description: Water channels made of this protein punch tiny pores in membranes, letting water cross about ten times faster than plain diffusion. Mice missing it lose 35% of body mass under water deprivation, yet Colton-null humans with the same defect feel nothing. The drought-surviving frog credited with a supercharged version has never had its actual AQP1 cloned or tested in any lab. In lungfish, the closer real data point, AQP1 activity drops during dry-season dormancy instead of rising.
Mechanism: Constitutively active water-selective tetrameric channel; ubiquitous in mammals.
Achievements (effect sizes): AQP1 generally: Preston 1992 (Agre) Xenopus-oocyte Pf 10–20× rise. Ma/Verkman 1998: AQP1-KO mice have 5–8× reduced proximal tubule Pf, 35% body-mass loss on water deprivation; urine osmolality 1081→505 mOsm. Colton-null humans subclinical. Cyclorana-SPECIFIC AQP1 has NOT been cloned or functionally characterized — source-organism work is whole-animal (bladder storage up to 50–60% body mass; plasma 487 mOsm/kg during 15-month estivation; Cartledge 2008). Desiccation tolerance is cocoon + metabolic depression + AQP2-type skin channels + urea, not AQP1 alone.
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 for mammalian endogenous AQP1 (Colton-null); T0–T1 for Cyclorana-specific AQP1
Translational Gaps: Entire frog-AQP-enhancement chain is missing: Cyclorana AQP cDNA not published; no heterologous expression in mammalian systems.
Key References (DOIs): Preston Science 1992 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.256.5055.385 | Ma JBC 1998 https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.8.4296 | Cartledge Physiol Biochem Zool 2008 https://doi.org/10.1086/588489
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTION to more-AQP1=more-retention model: lungfish aqp1 mRNA DECREASES during aestivation induction (Chng 2016) — opposite direction. Colton-null humans are asymptomatic → gain-of-function unlikely to be dramatic. Mammalian AQP1 phenotype is mild at baseline.

Narrative: Bats carry deadly viruses (Ebola, SARS-CoV-2, Nipah) without getting sick — a superpower rooted in their unique immune system. Bat ASC2 is a PYD-only protein that potently suppresses inflammasome assembly, preventing the runaway inflammation that kills other mammals during viral infection. Four key amino acid substitutions make bat ASC2 dramatically more effective than its human counterpart, representing an evolutionary solution to the inflammation-longevity tradeoff.
Short Description: Bats hold their inflammatory alarm below the level where it damages their own tissue, which is why flight and constant virus exposure do not cook them from the inside. Four bat-specific amino acids make their version about ten times better at this than the human one. Transgenic mice carrying it survived influenza A better and shrugged off gout crystals and SARS-CoV-2 inflammation. Paratus Sciences raised $100M on it, though capping inflammation is also how you get immunosuppressed.
Mechanism: ASC2 competitively binds NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasome PYD domains, blocking ASC speck formation and preventing caspase-1 activation and IL-1beta/IL-18 release. Four bat-specific residues (compared to human ASC2) confer ~10x stronger inhibition, effectively capping the inflammatory response below tissue-damaging thresholds.
Achievements (effect sizes): Transgenic mice expressing bat ASC2 showed reduced gout-crystal peritonitis, dampened multi-virus inflammation, reduced influenza A mortality, and suppressed SARS-CoV-2 inflammasome activation. Paratus Sciences launched with $100M to develop ASC2-inspired therapeutics.
Translational Gaps: Human ASC2 exists but is far weaker; gene therapy would need to deliver the bat-specific variant. Risk of immunosuppression. Paratus Sciences PS-1001 compound in preclinical development.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: $100M commercial validation (Paratus Sciences). Strongest commercial interest among new genes.

Narrative: Bdelloid rotifers survive radiation doses that would kill any vertebrate — partly thanks to a DNA repair enzyme they stole from bacteria. AvLigE is a prokaryotic DNA Ligase E acquired by horizontal gene transfer from bacteria into the rotifer Adineta vaga genome. When expressed in human cells, it significantly improves their radiation tolerance. This is evolution's most dramatic example of borrowing survival tools across the tree of life.
Short Description: Patches broken single strands in DNA after radiation damage, sealing breaks other repair enzymes leave open. Originally stolen from bacteria by a rotifer that survives radiation doses lethal to any vertebrate. Tested only in human cell lines in a dish, never in a living person. Because it's bacterial, it may not coordinate with the cell's own damage-signaling checkpoints, so its long-term behavior in a whole organism is untested.
Mechanism: AvLigE is a prokaryotic-type DNA ligase that catalyzes the final step of base excision repair and single-strand break repair. Its bacterial origin gives it distinct substrate preferences from eukaryotic ligases, providing complementary DNA repair capacity. In A. vaga, it is strongly upregulated after ionizing radiation exposure.
Achievements (effect sizes): Heterologous expression of AvLigE in human cell lines significantly improved radiation tolerance. Proteomic analysis confirmed it is a major DNA break repair contributor in irradiated rotifers. The gene was horizontally transferred from a prokaryote and is stably integrated in the rotifer genome.
Translational Gaps: Long-term effects of expressing a bacterial enzyme in human cells unknown. Integration with existing mammalian DNA repair pathways needs characterization. Potential interference with normal DNA damage signaling.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: One of very few demonstrated cases of a horizontally transferred gene directly improving human cell function.

Narrative: Tardigrades can dry out completely, sit in a dusty drawer for years, and revive in a drop of water. The CAHS proteins are a big part of that trick. When water leaves the cell, CAHS D doesn't just stabilize molecules — it phase-separates into a glass-like mesh, freezing the cell's contents in place until rehydration. University of Wyoming researchers expressed CAHS D in human HEK293 cells in 2022; under osmotic shock, the protein formed the predicted reversible fibers inside human cells, slowed their metabolism, and modestly improved survival. But the story has gotten complicated fast. Piszkiewicz 2019 showed that plenty of unrelated proteins protect enzymes from drying just as well. Ramirez 2023 found that CAHS D doesn't actually hold onto water in the dry state, refuting a popular model. Non-gelling variants sometimes protect better than gelling ones. The protein is real and does something; nobody quite agrees on what.
Short Description: When water leaves the cell, this protein self-assembles into a glass-like mesh that locks enzymes in place until rehydration reverses it. Adding it to yeast boosted desiccation survival roughly 100-fold. Human HEK293 cells making it form the same fibers under osmotic shock and survive slightly better, but no mouse or long-term mammalian data exist. The catch: non-gelling versions protect enzymes better than the gel-forming original, so the mesh may not be the active ingredient.
Mechanism: Intrinsically disordered tardigrade-specific protein; reversible concentration/temperature-dependent gel/fibril networks; molecular shield against desiccation-induced unfolding.
Achievements (effect sizes): Boothby 2017 Mol Cell: yeast expressing CAHS D ~100× increased desiccation survival; E. coli also protected; RNAi of CAHS in tardigrades reduced post-desiccation survival. In vitro: protects LDH, lipoprotein lipase. Tanaka 2022 PLOS Biol (HEp-2, HEK293T): CAHS 1/3/8/12 form reversible filaments under hyperosmotic stress, stiffen cells (AFM), and modestly improve survival. Sanchez-Martinez 2024 Protein Sci (HEK293): CAHS D fibers slow metabolism and improve survival after 0.5 M sorbitol shock. Gel point ~8–20 g/L.
Translational Gaps: Stable long-term mammalian desiccation survival not shown; no mouse data; Esterly 2020 showed only safety in mice, not efficacy.
Key References (DOIs): Yamaguchi PLoS ONE 2012 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0044209 | Boothby Mol Cell 2017 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2017.02.018 | Piszkiewicz Protein Sci 2019 https://doi.org/10.1002/pro.3604 | Tanaka PLoS Biol 2022 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3001780
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTIONS: (1) Piszkiewicz 2019 — many unrelated globular/disordered proteins protect LDH similarly, CAHS specificity challenged. (2) Ramirez 2023 — CAHS D does NOT retain water in dry state, refutes water-replacement/retention model. (3) Gel-vs-protection mechanism contested: Sanchez-Martinez 2024 shows non-gelling variants protect citrate synthase BETTER than gelling WT. (4) Tanaka 2023 reply — GFP-only controls also form mesh in drying tardigrades; "filaments" may not be CAHS-specific in vivo. Non-physiological overexpression; modest mammalian-cell effects.

Narrative: A gecko can hang from a glass ceiling by a single toe because its foot-pads are covered in millions of microscopic hairs — setae — each tipped with even finer spatulas. The contact area gets so large that van der Waals forces alone are enough. No glue, no suction. The 2015 Gekko japonicus genome revealed a family of about 72 beta-keratin genes that make these setae, with bursts of duplication around 100 and 85 million years ago — matching the evolutionary origins of gecko adhesion. A single seta generates 20 to 40 micronewtons of force, and a whole foot can hold 40 times the animal's body weight. Synthetic gecko-inspired tapes, from polymer microfibers to carbon-nanotube arrays, already work reasonably well. But expressing gecko beta-keratins in mammalian cells to grow actual setae is a non-starter: the adhesion depends on a hierarchical anatomy — cells, pillars, hairs, spatulas — built by a developmental program, not on the protein sequence itself.
Short Description: Millions of hair-thin setae on gecko toes fan into spatula tips so small that van der Waals attraction alone locks them to glass, no glue, no suction. One seta pulls 20-40 micronewtons, letting a foot support 40 times the gecko's body weight. This only works in Gekko japonicus, whose genome shows 72 beta-keratin genes shaping the setae, and zero attempts to express them in other cells have grown a working spatula. The trick is architecture, not protein: skin must build hairs-on-hairs first.
Mechanism: Large multigene family (~71–72 CBPs); polymerize into ~3–4 nm β-sheet filaments in oberhautchen/beta-layer cells → setae → spatular tips (~200–500 nm); adhesion is PURELY van der Waals.
Achievements (effect sizes): Liu 2015 Nat Commun: G. japonicus genome (2.55 Gb); 72 CBP genes mapped to setae; phylogenetic expansions ~105–96 Mya and ~87–80 Mya. Alibardi IHC: Ge-cprp-9 in setae/spatular tips. Autumn 2000 Nature: single seta 20–40 μN; whole foot holds ~40× body weight. Autumn 2002 PNAS: van der Waals confirmed on polar + nonpolar surfaces; synthetic PDMS/polyester spatulae reproduce adhesion. ZERO heterologous CBP transfer producing functional setae. Gecko tape (Geim 2003 Nat Mater) + CNT gecko tapes (Qu 2008 Science) are SYNTHETIC — no protein, no gene.
Translational Gaps: Gene transfer essentially a category error — adhesion requires hierarchical nanoarchitecture from developmental program, not compositional.
Key References (DOIs): Autumn Nature 2000 https://doi.org/10.1038/35015073 | Autumn PNAS 2002 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.192252799 | Liu Nat Commun 2015 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms10033 | Geim Nat Mater 2003 https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat917
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Setae also contain lipids + α-keratins. CBP count disputed (26 vs 72 annotations) — underannotated repetitive family. Adhesion requires hierarchical nanoarchitecture from developmental program — not compositional.

Narrative: The Egyptian mongoose attacks cobras with impunity, and the molecular secret fits in a single amino acid change. Snake alpha-neurotoxins kill by binding the muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) at the alpha-1 subunit, paralyzing the diaphragm and causing death by suffocation. Drabeck and colleagues showed in 2015 that mongooses, honey badgers, hedgehogs, and pigs have independently acquired amino acid substitutions at position 187 in the toxin-binding site of CHRNA1 that prevent alpha-neurotoxin binding through two mechanisms: introduction of an N-glycosylation motif (F187N in mongooses, adding a bulky sugar that blocks the toxin) or a positive charge (Y187R in honey badgers, electrostatically repelling the toxin). In 2022, Drabeck expanded the survey to find at least 13 independent instances of convergent venom resistance across all mammals — one of the most frequently convergently evolved traits known. Crucially, these single amino acid changes do not impair normal acetylcholine signaling. The receptor still conducts neurotransmission perfectly. This makes CHRNA1 F187N an ideal base editing target: one nucleotide change, minimal off-target risk, and the adaptation has been validated by natural selection in over a dozen independent mammalian lineages.
Short Description: A single swapped amino acid hangs a sugar group over the docking site cobra neurotoxins aim for, so the toxin slides off while ordinary nerve signalling continues untouched. Evolution has run this exact experiment at least 13 separate times across mammals, and 25 more in Australian skinks. Every case is a natural variant, since nobody has base-edited an animal and tested it against venom. It stops elapid neurotoxins only, not viper hemotoxins.
Mechanism: The F187N substitution introduces an N-linked glycosylation sequon at the alpha-neurotoxin binding site of the nAChR alpha-1 subunit. The attached N-glycan sterically blocks alpha-bungarotoxin and cobra neurotoxin binding. Alternative Y187R introduces positive charge that electrostatically repels cationic toxin. Both leave acetylcholine binding and channel gating intact.
Achievements (effect sizes): Drabeck 2015 Toxicon: convergent nAChR mutations in mongoose (F187N), honey badger (Y187R), hedgehog, pig — two distinct biochemical resistance mechanisms. Drabeck 2022 Biol Lett: 13 independent convergent evolution events across mammals under positive selection. Chandrasekara 2025: 25 additional instances in Australian skinks, binding assays confirming resistance.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mammalian natural variants + functional binding assays)
Translational Gaps: No engineered base-editing demonstration — all evidence from natural variants. In-vivo venom challenge in edited animals not performed. Protection specific to alpha-neurotoxins — does not cover hemotoxic, cytotoxic, or phospholipase venoms.
Key References (DOIs): Drabeck Toxicon 2015 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.toxicon.2015.03.007 | Drabeck Biol Lett 2022 https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2022.0361
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Protects ONLY against alpha-neurotoxins (elapid snake venom) — not viper hemotoxins, bee venom, or other mechanisms. Practical utility is narrow: relevant for people in cobra/krait/mamba habitats or military/fieldwork in tropical regions. The beauty is evolutionary validation — nature has run this exact experiment 13+ times and the edit always works without breaking the receptor.

Narrative: Bowhead whales live past 200 years in Arctic waters without ever seeming to get cancer. In 2025, the Rochester group found that bowheads express a stress-response protein called CIRBP at roughly a hundred times human levels, and that the whale version is unusually stable. When they put bowhead CIRBP into human cells, DNA-break repair efficiency jumped 1.6-fold, with fewer of the chromosomal errors (micronuclei) that cancer cells accumulate. Expressing it in fruit flies extended their lifespan by about 20%. The mechanism looks less like bulletproof defense and more like meticulous proofreading — when damage happens, the whale cell fixes it right the first time, instead of leaving sloppy scars. There's an uncomfortable paradox: bowhead cells actually need fewer cancer mutations to transform than mouse cells do. They don't resist cancer by being hard to break; they resist it by being impossibly good at fixing the break.
Short Description: This protein patrols broken DNA strands and glues them back together cleanly, cutting the sloppy repairs that let cells turn cancerous. Bowhead whales make ~100 times more of it than humans, and adding it to human cells boosted DNA-break repair 1.6-fold. So far it has only extended lifespan in fruit flies, about 20%, with no mouse or human trial. The same protein leaks out as eCIRP, an inflammatory signal driving sepsis and fuelling liver and breast cancer.
Mechanism: Cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (~18 kDa) with RRM + Gly-rich domain; localizes to DSBs; promotes Ku70/80 loading, stimulates XRCC4-LigIV end-joining; bowhead C-terminus confers enhanced protein stability; damage-site enrichment is RNase-A-sensitive.
Achievements (effect sizes): Firsanov/Seluanov/Gorbunova 2025 Nature: bwCIRBP ~100× higher protein abundance in bowhead vs human/mouse. Expression of bwCIRBP in HUMAN CELLS enhanced NHEJ + HR efficiency ~1.6-fold; reduced micronuclei; purified protein stimulated in-vitro end-joining; Ku binding promoted. Drosophila overexpression of either bwCIRBP or hCIRBP extended lifespan ~20% and improved IR survival. Bowhead fibroblasts show higher DSB-repair fidelity and lower mutation rate.
Translational Gaps: Mouse Tg lifespan/cancer study; AAV/LNP delivery; safety vs eCIRP inflammatory pathway.
Key References (DOIs): Firsanov Nature 2025 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09694-5 | Qiang Nat Med 2013 https://doi.org/10.1038/nm.3368
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: PARADOX: bowhead fibroblasts require FEWER oncogenic hits for transformation (cancer resistance is via repair fidelity, not barrier strength). CIRBP has DUAL ROLES: extracellular CIRP (eCIRP) is a pro-inflammatory DAMP in sepsis/I-R injury (Qiang 2013); CIRBP has pro-tumorigenic roles in HCC/breast cancer — context-dependent. Identity of the causal longevity factor is one of many differentially expressed (RPA2 also ↑).

Narrative: Dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time — one hemisphere stays awake, so they never stop swimming or breathing. The molecular question is whether this is hardwired into the genes of their circadian clock. Yin et al. in 2025 took the cetacean-specific amino-acid changes and dropped them into zebrafish Clock and Bmal1 proteins, then bred transgenic larvae: the mutant fish slept significantly less, stayed alert longer, and upregulated wake-promoting glutamate signaling while downregulating the sleep-promoting GABA and acetylcholine networks. That's a real result — a cell-autonomous piece of the sleep rewiring — but it's also a toe in the water, not a leg. The actual dolphin genes have never been knocked into a mammal. Zebrafish don't have unihemispheric sleep, and hemispheric asymmetry is almost certainly a brain-network property, not something you can install in a cell culture. The clock mutations look like one ingredient in a much larger recipe.
Short Description: This gene pair sets the daily rhythm telling cells when to wake and sleep. Dolphin-style substitutions in zebrafish larvae cut sleep, add wake bouts, shorten sleep bouts (p<0.0001), raise wake-driving glutamate genes, lower sleep-driving GABA genes. Only ever done in zebrafish carrying dolphin-style mutations, never the real dolphin gene or any mammal. Dolphins' actual trick, sleeping with half the brain at once, is brain-network wiring one gene swap in fish can't reproduce.
Mechanism: bHLH-PAS circadian transcription factors; cetacean-specific substitutions alter nuclear localization and TF activation.
Achievements (effect sizes): Yin 2025 PLOS Genet: cetacean-specific substitutions introduced into ZEBRAFISH Clocka/Bmal1a backbone. Luciferase per1b promoter reporter: Clocka-mut and Bmal1a-mut significantly enhanced transactivation. Nuclear localization increased; Co-IP showed stronger heterodimer (p=0.0184). Zebrafish larvae overexpressing mutants (n=40–46) had significantly reduced sleep, shorter bouts, more wake bouts (p<0.0001). Transcriptome: ↑glutamatergic wakefulness genes; ↓GABAergic/cholinergic sleep genes.
Translational Gaps: Mouse knock-in; EEG/hemispheric resolution study; unihemispheric sleep is not a cell-autonomous phenotype.
Key References (DOIs): Yin PLoS Genet 2025 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1011598
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: NOT the actual dolphin gene — mutations introduced on zebrafish backbone at homologous positions; zebrafish don't exhibit USWS; no mammalian validation. Same group's Bai 2024 SLEEP: BMAL2 (not BMAL1) K204E/K346Q enhances PER2 activation in zebrafish — three different clock genes (CLOCK, BMAL1, BMAL2) all claimed to adapt, overlapping claims unresolved. USWS is widely viewed as network/neuroanatomical, not cell-autonomous.

Narrative: The deathstalker scorpion's sting contains a 36-amino-acid peptide called chlorotoxin that evolution designed to kill — but oncologists are using it to find and treat brain tumors. Chlorotoxin selectively binds chloride channels and matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) on the surface of glioma cells with remarkable specificity, while ignoring normal brain tissue. Mamelak and colleagues ran Phase I/II clinical trials in 2006 using iodine-131-labeled synthetic chlorotoxin (TM-601) injected directly into brain tumors of 18 glioma patients: the peptide bound to tumor periphery with long retention, one patient achieved partial response, and two were disease-free beyond 30 months. A next-generation version, tozuleristide (BLZ-100), conjugates chlorotoxin with a near-infrared fluorescent dye for real-time surgical tumor visualization. Patil and colleagues reported in 2019 that BLZ-100 was safe at doses up to 30 mg IV with fluorescence detected in both high- and low-grade gliomas. This is one of the most clinically advanced venom-derived peptides in medicine — a scorpion protein repurposed to paint cancers visible under a surgeon's lamp. The FDA granted orphan drug designation for pediatric brain tumor imaging.
Short Description: This 36-amino-acid scorpion peptide latches onto chloride channels and MMP-2 on glioma cell surfaces, blocking their migration into brain tissue. It killed glioma cells at IC50 0.28 μM versus 8 μM for normal astrocytes. Iodine-131-tagged versions reached human trials: 18 patients, one partial response, two disease-free past 30 months; a dye version, tozuleristide, now guides surgeons live. IV doses cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, so most delivery injects straight into the tumor.
Mechanism: Chlorotoxin is a 36-aa cystine-knot miniprotein with 4 disulfide bonds. It binds MMP-2 and chloride channels (ClC-3) overexpressed on glioma cell surfaces, inhibiting cell migration and invasion. Glioma selectivity correlates with annexin A2 expression. Conjugated to I-131 for targeted radiotherapy or ICG for fluorescence-guided surgery.
Achievements (effect sizes): Mamelak 2006 J Clin Oncol: Phase I/II 131I-TM-601 in 18 glioma patients — well tolerated, tumor-specific binding, 1 PR, 2 disease-free >30 months. Patil 2019 Neurosurgery: BLZ-100 Phase I safe at 30 mg IV, fluorescence in gliomas, no DLTs. Fu 2006: recombinant CTX IC50 ~0.28 μM in glioma vs ~8 μM in normal astrocytes.
Translational Gaps: Glioma selectivity mechanism incompletely understood. Full regulatory approval not yet achieved. IV systemic delivery crosses BBB with limited efficiency. Non-brain tumor applications less validated.
Key References (DOIs): Mamelak J Clin Oncol 2006 https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2005.05.4569 | Patil Neurosurgery 2019 https://doi.org/10.1093/neuros/nyz125 | Fu Neurosci Lett 2006 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neulet.2006.10.056
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: While chlorotoxin is a scorpion venom component, the therapeutic versions are synthetic peptides — no actual venom production is involved. BLZ-100/tozuleristide (Blaze Bioscience) is the most clinically advanced chlorotoxin conjugate. The binding mechanism via annexin A2 and MMP-2 is still debated — specificity correlates with but may not be perfectly selective for malignant tissue.

Narrative: Every time you get a sunburn, ultraviolet light is welding your DNA bases together — creating cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) that cause mutations and eventually skin cancer. Humans repair this damage slowly through nucleotide excision repair. But there's a faster fix that evolution took away from us: photolyase, a light-activated enzyme that directly reverses CPDs in a single catalytic step. All plants, bacteria, fungi, and most vertebrates have it — but placental mammals lost the gene around 170 million years ago. Marsupials still have it. The long-nosed potoroo carries a functional class II CPD photolyase, and when Jans and colleagues put it into transgenic mice in 2005, the result was remarkable: powerful resistance to UV-induced skin cancer, with dramatically reduced sunburn, apoptosis, hyperplasia, and mutation. Boros and colleagues went further in 2013, delivering marsupial photolyase to human keratinocytes via pseudouridine-modified mRNA — the same technology as COVID vaccines — and demonstrated functional CPD repair, reduced IL-6 inflammation, and rescued cell proliferation after UVB exposure. This is one of the cleanest lost-gene-restoration stories in biology: we once had this gene, we lost it in the nocturnal mammal bottleneck, and we can put it back using mRNA.
Short Description: This enzyme grabs UV-fused DNA bases in skin cells and, lit by blue light, splits them apart in one step, undoing damage that causes sunburn and cancer. In 2005 mice with this potoroo gene showed near-total blockage of UV sunburn, apoptosis, and tumor-causing mutations. In 2013 the gene, delivered as mRNA, repaired UV damage in human skin cells using the same platform later used for COVID vaccines. No human trial exists, and it can't fix DNA in deeper dermis, where light never reaches.
Mechanism: CPD photolyase binds cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer lesions in DNA and, upon absorption of blue/UV-A light (300–500 nm), uses an FAD cofactor to transfer an electron that splits the cyclobutane ring, restoring the two pyrimidines to their undamaged state in a single catalytic step.
Achievements (effect sizes): Jans 2005 Curr Biol: CPD-photolyase transgenic mice showed powerful resistance to UV-induced skin tumorigenesis. Nearly all acute UV responses (sunburn, apoptosis, hyperplasia, mutation) were CPD-dependent and blocked. Boros 2013: pseudouridine-mRNA photolyase in human keratinocytes — reduced CPDs, IL-6, rescued proliferation after UVB.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (transgenic mouse skin cancer prevention) + T6 (human keratinocyte mRNA delivery)
Translational Gaps: No human in-vivo trial. Photolyase requires visible light activation — deep skin layers may not receive sufficient light. mRNA delivery is transient. Potential interaction with melanin UV shielding unknown.
Key References (DOIs): Jans Curr Biol 2005 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2005.01.001 | Boros J Photochem Photobiol B 2013 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jphotobiol.2013.09.010 | Kavakli Adv Protein Chem Struct Biol 2019 https://doi.org/10.1016/bs.apcsb.2018.10.003
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Cosmetic products containing bacterial photolyase-liposomes exist (e.g., Eryfotona Actinica), but clinical efficacy is debated. The mRNA approach (Boros 2013) is more rigorous — produces intranuclear enzyme. Light-activation requirement is both a safety feature (only active in illuminated skin) and a limitation (cannot repair damage in deep dermis).

Narrative: Migratory birds find their way by sensing Earth's magnetic field through their eyes. The leading candidate for the magnetic sensor is CRY4a, a cryptochrome protein in retinal photoreceptors that generates short-lived radical pairs when blue light hits it, and those radical pairs respond weakly to magnetic fields. A 2021 Oxford-Oldenburg collaboration purified the European robin's CRY4a, recreated the radical pairs in a cuvette, and showed they were more magnetically sensitive than the chicken or pigeon versions — quantum biology you can measure in a test tube. The physics is gorgeous; the in vivo translation is shaky. Leberecht 2023 pointed out that mammalian cells contain FAD (the cofactor CRY needs) at nanomolar levels — orders of magnitude below what the radical-pair mechanism seems to require. A mammalian magnetic compass through CRY4 looks biochemically implausible. Pigeons also have magnetically sensitive CRY4 and aren't night-migrants, so the molecule alone isn't sufficient even in birds.
Short Description: Blue light hits this retinal protein and splits an electron pair into two radicals whose spin flips with Earth's magnetic field, letting the eye sense direction. Purified robin CRY4a showed larger magnetic effects than chicken or pigeon versions, but only above real geomagnetic strength. It exists only as an E. coli extract, with no animal gaining magnetic sense from it. Mammal cells hold its fuel FAD far below the dose the reaction needs.
Mechanism: Cryptochrome 4a (527 aa); FAD-based radical-pair magnetoreception via Trp-tetrad electron transfer (W395/W372/W318/W369); singlet/triplet interconversion modulated by geomagnetic field.
Achievements (effect sizes): Xu/Hore/Mouritsen 2021 Nature: purified recombinant ErCry4 (from E. coli) — photoinduced FAD/Trp radical pairs by transient absorption spectroscopy; magnetic field effects LARGER than chicken/pigeon CRY4 orthologs under identical conditions; Trp-tetrad mutants progressively abolish cascade. Effect sizes few-percent MFE at fields ABOVE geomagnetic. Retinal localization in outer segments of double-cone / LW single-cone; seasonal upregulation (correlative). Bartölke 2024: ErCry4a associates with ordered lipid bilayers.
Translational Gaps: No Tg mouse/fly/fish confers magnetoreception via CRY4.
Key References (DOIs): Xu Nature 2021 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03618-9 | Hochstoeger Sci Adv 2020 (pigeon CRY4) https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abb9110
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: MFEs at supra-geomagnetic fields; radical-pair lifetime in vivo may be too short; no transduction partners identified. Pigeon CRY4 (Hochstoeger 2020) also magnetically sensitive yet pigeons are not night-migratory. BIOCHEMICAL IMPLAUSIBILITY for mammals: Leberecht 2023 Front Physiol — mammalian FAD concentrations are NANOMOLAR, far below µM required to saturate Type-II CRYs → a mammalian radical-pair compass is biochemically implausible. Alternative magnetite-based trigeminal compass (Zapka 2009). MagR alternative (Qin 2016) unreplicated.

Narrative: The scaly-foot snail (Chrysomallon squamiferum) is the only known animal that incorporates iron sulfide into its body armor — building scales of greigite and pyrite at hydrothermal vents. Its biomineralization gene toolkit mediates biologically controlled iron sulfide nanoparticle formation at temperatures where industrial synthesis requires extreme heat. This living foundry turns dissolved metal ions into organized armor.
Short Description: Channel-like columns in the scale skin pump out sulfur, which grabs iron ions and locks them into greigite and pyrite crystals, building metal armor plates. This iron-sulfide trick works at a mild 15°C, while industrial versions of these crystals need extreme heat. So far it's only ever been done in the scaly-foot snail at hydrothermal vents. Twenty-five separate transcription factors run this pathway, so no single gene transfer can replicate the armor.
Mechanism: The CSMG biomineralization toolkit involves channel-like protein columns in the scale epithelium that supply biogenic sulfur, which reacts with environmental iron ions to form greigite (Fe3S4) and pyrite (FeS2) nanoparticles. The genome reveals 25 transcription factors controlling independent scale and shell mineralization pathways, with many shared with other lophotrochozoan biomineralizers.
Achievements (effect sizes): Iron sulfide nanoparticle formation demonstrated at ~15°C in controlled experiments. Genome sequenced (444.4 Mb) revealing independent transcription factor sets for scale vs shell. The only known metazoan using iron-sulfide biomineralization.
Translational Gaps: Multi-gene pathway makes single-gene transfer insufficient. The vent environment provides unique chemistry. Industrial bioreactor conditions for iron-sulfide biomineralization need development.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Unique biology — only metazoan with iron-sulfide incorporation. Applications in nanoparticle synthesis and bio-inspired materials.

Narrative: Tardigrades survive doses of radiation that would vaporize a human — and they carry a protein called Dsup that drapes itself over DNA like a molecular bodyguard. When Japanese researchers put Dsup into human HEK293 kidney cells in 2016, the cells shrugged off X-ray damage that would normally shred their chromosomes, with DNA breaks cut roughly in half at 10 Gy. In 2025, an MIT/Dana-Farber team used lipid nanoparticles — the same delivery system as COVID vaccines — to briefly paint Dsup onto mouse mouth and rectal tissue during radiotherapy, sparing healthy cells while still killing the tumor. That's the first real demonstration of tardigrade radioprotection in a living mammal. The catch: in rat cortical neurons, Dsup did the opposite, causing more DNA damage, not less. The bodyguard works in some cells and goes rogue in others, and nobody yet knows why.
Short Description: Draped over chromosomes, this tardigrade protein blocks radicals and radiation from shredding DNA, halving X-ray damage in human kidney cells at 10 Gy. In 2025 mRNA in lipid nanoparticles painted it onto mouse mouth and rectal tissue during radiotherapy, sparing healthy cells while tumours still died. That was the first live-mammal proof, and no transgenic mouse or human trial exists. In rat neurons it backfired, causing more DNA breaks instead of fewer.
Mechanism: Intrinsically disordered nucleosome-binding protein (HMGN-like C-terminal motif per Chavez 2019, revised from Hashimoto 2016 direct-DNA model); shields chromatin from hydroxyl radicals and ionizing radiation.
Achievements (effect sizes): HEK293 at 10 Gy X-ray: comet tail DNA 33%→16% (~50% SSB reduction); H2O2: 71%→18%. Replicated in CHO, Drosophila, tobacco (UV-B recovery), yeast (longevity under H2O2). C. elegans: protection at 90 Gy X-ray without toxicity. Proton IR protection at 150 MeV. Rajesh/Kirtane 2025 Nat Biomed Eng: LNP-Dsup mRNA delivered to mouse buccal/rectal mucosa during radiotherapy reduced γH2AX and comet damage in peritumoral tissue while preserving tumor kill — first in-vivo mammalian demonstration.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (transient mRNA/LNP 2025) + T6 (≥4 independent labs) + T3 (C. elegans)
Translational Gaps: Germline transgenic mouse; durable delivery; heavy-ion/LET data; long-term mutagenesis surveillance; CNS-safe variant.
Key References (DOIs): Hashimoto Nat Commun 2016 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms12808 | Chavez eLife 2019 https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.47682 | Escarcega Mol Cell Neurosci 2023 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mcn.2023.103826 | Kirtane/Rajesh Nat Biomed Eng 2025 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41551-025-01360-5
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTION: Escarcega 2023 — Dsup PROMOTED DSBs, chromatin condensation, and neurotoxicity in rat cortical neurons — opposite phenotype in CNS. Hashimoto direct-DNA-binding model superseded by nucleosome-binding (Chavez 2019). HEK293 protection is ~2-fold at best; no stable transgenic mouse. Basal chromatin perturbation and cell-type specificity unknown.

Narrative: Tibetans live above 13,000 feet without the thick-blood sickness that plagues lowlanders who move to altitude. The cause is one of the most spectacular finds in human genetics: a 32-kilobase chunk of DNA, carrying the hypoxia-sensor gene EPAS1, that Tibetans inherited from Denisovans — an extinct hominin known only from a finger bone in a Siberian cave. The variant dampens EPAS1's response to low oxygen, so red blood cell counts stay safe instead of spiraling up. Tibetans with the adaptive version carry about 0.8 g/dL less hemoglobin at 4,200 meters. Knocking out the equivalent enhancer in human endothelial cells and in mice reproduces the blunted response. The same locus is a double-edged sword: gain-of-function mutations nearby cause Pacak-Zhuang syndrome (runaway blood production plus tumors), and Andean highlanders achieved a similar outcome through a completely different mutation — a textbook case of evolution finding two roads to the same summit.
Short Description: This gene senses low oxygen and signals more red blood cells; the Tibetan version dials that down, keeping blood thinner at altitude. Adaptive homozygotes at 4,200 meters carry about 0.8 g/dL less hemoglobin, inherited as a 32-kb Denisovan DNA chunk now in 72–87% of Tibetans. It's only been deleted in human heart and blood-vessel cells and mice, never installed in a human. Nearby gain-of-function mutations in the same gene instead cause Pacak-Zhuang syndrome: erythrocytosis plus tumors.
Mechanism: Noncoding cis-regulatory hypomorph blunts hypoxic HIF-2α induction → lower EPO → lower Hb, lower pulmonary artery pressure, chronic-mountain-sickness protection.
Achievements (effect sizes): Huerta-Sánchez 2014 Nature: 32.7-kb Tibetan haplotype exact match to Altai Denisovan (D-stat p=0.006); absent in non-East-Asian 1000G; adaptive frequency 72–87% vs 2–9% Han. Beall 2010 PNAS: ~0.8 g/dL Hb reduction in adaptive homozygotes at 4,200 m. Peng 2017 MBE: ~2.87% Hb variance per SNP; Epas1+/− mice phenocopy blunted Hb and reduced PA pressure. Gray 2022 Sci Adv: CRISPR deletion of ENH5 enhancer in human endothelial and cardiomyocyte cells + mice recapitulates blunted hypoxic EPAS1.
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (population genetics) + T6 (CRISPR human cells) + T5 (KO/enhancer-KO mice)
Translational Gaps: Tibetan-allele knock-in mouse; low-altitude healthspan data; clinical trial of belzutifan-like HIF-2α inhibitors for chronic mountain sickness (underway).
Key References (DOIs): Huerta-Sánchez Nature 2014 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13408 | Beall PNAS 2010 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1002443107 | Peng MBE 2017 https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msx194 | Gray Sci Adv 2022 https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abn7342 | Zhuang NEJM 2012 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1205119
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: BIDIRECTIONAL LOCUS: Gain-of-function missense mutations (A530S, Y532C etc. near Pro531) cause Pacak-Zhuang syndrome (erythrocytosis + paraganglioma + pheochromocytoma). Andeans achieve a similar phenotype via a CODING missense — convergent direction, divergent mechanism. All selected Tibetan SNPs noncoding; each ~2–3% Hb variance; no Tibetan-allele knock-in mouse yet.

Narrative: Six fish lineages independently evolved electric organs — the electric catfish (Malapterurus electricus) generates up to 350V from a single-celled-thick electric organ wrapping its body. The electrogenesis program involves coordinated regulation of ion channels (Nav1.4a, Kv), transcription factors, and structural proteins that convert muscle cells into electrocytes. This convergent evolution across 100+ million years reveals a deeply conserved 'electric toolkit' in vertebrate genomes.
Short Description: Muscle cells stop contracting and line up like living batteries, shutting off myosin and actin while loading one membrane face with sodium and potassium channels. This one-cell-thick organ fires up to 350 volts, evolved independently six times in fish over 100+ million years. It exists only in the electric catfish and kin — no synthetic version, no human trial. Converting muscle needs dozens of genes rewired at once, so no single gene transfer can switch it on.
Mechanism: Electrocyte differentiation involves suppression of contractile genes (myosin, actin) and upregulation of ion channels (scn4aa/Nav1.4a for sodium, kcna7a for potassium). A duplicated sodium channel gene lost muscle expression through cis-regulatory changes and gained electric organ-specific expression. Acetylcholine receptors cluster on one face, creating the membrane asymmetry needed for voltage generation.
Achievements (effect sizes): Six independent origins of electric organs identified. Convergent gene expression patterns across lineages (2014 Science). Electric catfish chromosome-level genome assembled (797 Mb, 28 chromosomes). Sodium channel evolution from muscle to electric organ characterized.
Translational Gaps: Multi-gene program makes single-gene transfer insufficient. Electric organ development requires specific tissue architecture. Synthetic biology approaches to engineer electrocytes from muscle cells are early-stage.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Convergent evolution across 6 lineages spanning 100+ million years. No therapeutic application; fundamental biology and bio-inspired engineering.

Narrative: What if aging isn't one disease but a cascade of interconnected failures — and you could treat several at once with a single injection? In 2019, Noah Davidsohn and George Church's group at the Wyss Institute tested exactly that. They packaged three longevity-associated genes — FGF21, αKlotho, and a soluble decoy of TGF-beta receptor 2 (sTGFβR2) — into separate AAV vectors and delivered them to mice modelling obesity, diabetes, heart failure, and kidney disease. A single combination of just FGF21 plus sTGFβR2 treated all four conditions simultaneously: heart function improved 58%, kidney fibrosis marker αSMA dropped 38%, renal atrophy fell 75%, and obesity with diabetes was completely reversed in high-fat-diet mice. FGF21 alone had already been shown to extend lifespan — Zhang et al. in 2012 demonstrated that FGF21-transgenic mice lived about 36% longer by suppressing the growth-hormone/IGF-1 axis, mimicking caloric restriction without eating less. The TGFβR2 decoy mops up excess TGF-beta signalling, the master driver of fibrosis in aged kidneys, livers, and hearts. The catch: Davidsohn's study used disease-specific mouse models, not natural aging, and the AAV doses were high. Whether one shot in middle age can genuinely extend healthy lifespan in normal mice remains untested.
Short Description: This liver hormone shuts down growth signalling and burns fat, while a decoy receptor mops up scarring signals in heart and kidneys. Combined, one shot reversed obesity and diabetes in fat-fed mice, cut kidney scarring 75% and lifted heart function 58%. It has only been tested in disease-model mice by Rejuvenate Bio, the founders' own company, now running dog trials. FGF21 alone added 36% lifespan, but those mice were 20% smaller with weaker bones.
Mechanism: FGF21: hepatokine (181 aa) signalling via FGFR1c/β-Klotho; suppresses GH/IGF-1 axis, enhances insulin sensitivity, promotes fatty acid oxidation. sTGFβR2: soluble decoy receptor sequestering TGF-β1/β3; blocks SMAD2/3 phosphorylation → reduces fibroblast activation, collagen deposition, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition.
Achievements (effect sizes): Davidsohn 2019 PNAS: AAV-FGF21 + AAV-sTGFβR2 in C57BL/6 mice: heart failure model → 58% improvement in fractional shortening; kidney fibrosis → 38% reduction in αSMA, 75% reduction in renal atrophy; HFD obesity/diabetes → complete reversal. Zhang 2012 eLife: FGF21-Tg mice median lifespan +36% (females ~46 vs ~34 months); mechanism via blunting GH/IGF-1.
Translational Gaps: Natural-aging lifespan study with combination not published; AAV dose optimisation; immunogenicity of chronic sTGFβR2; FGF21 resistance in metabolically stressed humans; human FGF21 analogues (pegbelfermin) showed mixed phase II results for NASH.
Key References (DOIs): Davidsohn PNAS 2019 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1910073116 | Zhang eLife 2012 https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.00065
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: FGF21 lifespan extension correlated with SUPPRESSED GH/IGF-1 axis — FGF21-Tg mice had reduced body size (~20% smaller) and bone loss; effectively a caloric-restriction mimic with growth penalty. Davidsohn 2019 used disease-SPECIFIC models, NOT natural aging. sTGFβR2 blocks a pathway essential for immune regulation and wound healing — chronic suppression could impair anti-tumour immunity. FGF21 resistance reported in obese/inflamed humans. Church/Davidsohn co-founded Rejuvenate Bio (conflict of interest noted). No independent replication of the combination therapy. COMMERCIAL STATUS: Rejuvenate Bio (https://www.rejuvenatebio.com/), co-founded by George Church and Noah Davidsohn, is pursuing an animal-health-first strategy with dog gene therapy trials before human applications. The combination therapy is not commercially available. Church lab conflict-of-interest noted in the originating PNAS paper.

Narrative: A firefly lights up by burning a tiny molecule called luciferin. The enzyme luciferase is astonishingly efficient — about 41% of the chemical energy becomes visible photons, a quantum yield that human engineering cannot match. Put luciferase into a mouse tumor, inject luciferin, and you can count cancer cells through living tissue. Enhanced versions can track as few as three adoptively transferred T-cells. For decades it was the workhorse of biomedical imaging. The frontier now is autonomous bioluminescence — getting mammals to make their own luciferin so they glow without injections. Autonomous plants already exist (a 2020 fungal-pathway tobacco produces visible light on its own, ~10⁸ photons per second per plant), but mammals lack a key precursor. The dream of glowing tattoos or bioluminescent skin runs aground on the same problem that made GFP a lab tool and not a therapy: tissue absorbs visible light. A glowing human would glow, pharmacologically speaking, only skin-deep.
Short Description: Cells carrying this enzyme burn injected luciferin and glow, turning about 41% of that chemical energy into visible light, a yield no man-made bulb matches. Tagged T-cells let researchers track as few as 3 individual cells moving through a living mouse. It's a lab-imaging staple in mice and glowing tobacco plants, never approved for humans, who still rely on PET scans. Mammals lack the caffeic acid fireflies use, so a self-glowing human is blocked at fuel supply, not enzyme.
Mechanism: ATP+Mg+O2-dependent oxidation of D-luciferin → ~560 nm photon (QY ≈ 0.41).
Achievements (effect sizes): de Wet 1987: firefly luc in mammalian cells. Ow 1986 Science: first glowing tobacco (exogenous luciferin spray). Tg luc+ mice are a staple — IVIS imaging after 150 mg/kg IP D-luciferin; detect tumors from ~1,000 cells. Rabinovich 2008 PNAS: enhanced firefly luciferase (effLuc) expressed in mouse T-cells enabled bioluminescent tracking of as few as 3 individual cells in adoptive immunotherapy models. Close 2010/2018 PNAS: autonomous bacterial luxCDABEfrp in HEK293 cells — 12× background, visible at 25,000 cells with 10-min integration. Mitiouchkina 2020 Nat Biotechnol: fungal nnluz + hispS/h3h/npgA gene cluster from Neonothopanus nambi in tobacco → autonomous visible bioluminescence ~10^8–10^9 photons/s per plant (endogenous caffeic acid → luciferin).
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (human cells substrate-dep); T5 (mice, luciferin-dep); T3 (autonomous in plants); NOT fully autonomous in peer-reviewed mammals yet
Translational Gaps: In-human clinical imaging ceded to PET reporters; autonomous mammal germline line not peer-reviewed.
Key References (DOIs): de Wet Mol Cell Biol 1987 https://doi.org/10.1128/mcb.7.2.725-737.1987 | Ow Science 1986 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.234.4778.856 | Rabinovich PNAS 2008 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0804105105 | Mitiouchkina Nat Biotechnol 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-020-0500-9
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Classical system requires substrate injection; mammalian caffeic acid scarce → low autonomous flux; tissue absorption; ATP-coupled signal. Bacterial lux vs fungal luz debate — codon-optimized lux may outperform fungal in mammals lacking caffeic acid.

Narrative: If you had to bet on a single gene associated with human longevity, FOXO3 is the safest bet in biology. One variant of it (rs2802292) shows up across centenarian populations — Okinawan Japanese, German, Italian, American — in study after study. Willcox 2008 found that Hawaiian men homozygous for the longevity allele were 2.75 times more likely to reach 95 than the general population. FOXO3 is a stress-response conductor, switching on the cell's repair and recycling programs when things get rough. Here's the uncomfortable gap: despite being the strongest human genetic signal for long life besides APOE, no one has ever made a mouse overexpress FOXO3 and lived longer. The experiment that would close the loop — take the centenarian-linked gene, put it in a mammal, measure lifespan — has simply never been published. It's the biggest unopened box in the longevity genetics field.
Short Description: This gene flips on a cell's repair, recycling, and antioxidant genes like SOD2 and catalase when under strain. Okinawan men with two copies of the longevity variant were 2.75 times more likely to reach 95, replicated in German, Italian, and American cohorts. No mouse has ever been made to overexpress FOXO3 and shown to live longer — that lifespan study doesn't exist. Overexpressing it in mouse forebrain neurons killed them, and the same gene drives glioma and leukemia stem cells.
Mechanism: Stress-responsive transcription factor downstream of insulin/IGF-1 signaling; drives SOD2, catalase, GADD45, autophagy, p27.
Achievements (effect sizes): Willcox 2008 PNAS, Okinawan Hawaiian men: rs2802292 homozygotes OR 2.75 (95% CI 1.51–5.02) for age ≥95; heterozygotes OR 1.91. Replicated in German (Flachsbart 2009), Italian, CHARGE, ≥11 cohorts; meta-OR ~1.5. FOXO3 + APOE are the two reproducible longevity loci. Renault 2009: FoxO3-KO depletes adult neural stem cells. No published whole-mouse FOXO3 overexpression lifespan study.
Translational Gaps: The single largest gap in the library: NO mouse Tg FOXO3 overexpression lifespan data; no activator in trials; tissue-specific forebrain overexpression was neurotoxic (Arruda-Carvalho 2014).
Key References (DOIs): Willcox PNAS 2008 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0801030105 | Flachsbart PNAS 2009 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0809594106 | Broer J Gerontol A 2015 (CHARGE) https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glu166
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Effect is associative only; OR modest (~1.5 in meta); sex-specific (stronger in men, unexplained); FOXO3 is pro-oncogenic in glioma/AML stem cells (Sunayama 2011). Forebrain overexpression neurotoxic. The enhancement chain — human variant → mammalian gain-of-function → longevity — is NOT closed experimentally.

Narrative: Your muscles are locked in a tug-of-war between growth signals and a powerful brake called myostatin. Follistatin is nature's way of releasing that brake — it binds myostatin and neutralises it, unleashing muscle growth that is otherwise tightly suppressed. In 2009, Haidet and Bhatt at Nationwide Children's Hospital showed that a single intramuscular injection of AAV1-follistatin-344 increased muscle mass and grip strength in both normal and dystrophic mice, with quadriceps weight rising over 100% in some cohorts. In 2015, Mendell's group ran the first human trial: six boys with Becker muscular dystrophy received bilateral AAV1-FS344 injections into the quadriceps. The six-minute walk test improved by a mean of 58 metres at 24 months, with no serious adverse events and no detectable anti-myostatin antibodies. A 2017 follow-up in inclusion body myositis patients showed similar safety and modest functional benefit. The catch: follistatin also binds activins and other TGF-beta family members, meaning its effects are not muscle-specific — it influences reproductive hormones, inflammation, and fibrosis in ways that are hard to predict long-term.
Short Description: A secreted protein floods muscle with growth signals by mopping up myostatin, the brake that keeps fibres from bulking up. One AAV1 injection drove mouse quadriceps mass up over 100% and grip strength up 60%. Six Becker MD boys walked 58 metres farther at 24 months, and unlicensed plasmid versions now sell in Honduras and Panama for about $25,000 with nothing published. Follistatin also blocks activins, disrupting reproductive hormones.
Mechanism: Follistatin: 344-aa secreted glycoprotein; binds and neutralises myostatin (GDF-8), activin A/B, and GDF-11 with high affinity; blocks SMAD2/3 signalling through ActRIIB; relieves transcriptional repression of myogenic genes → satellite cell activation, myofiber hypertrophy.
Achievements (effect sizes): Haidet 2009 (AAV1-FS344 mouse): quadriceps mass +100% vs controls; grip strength +60% in mdx mice. Mendell 2015 (human phase I/IIa, n=6 Becker MD): 6-min walk +58 m at 24 months (3/6 patients improved >50 m); no SAEs; anti-AAV1 Abs present but no anti-myostatin Abs. Mendell 2017 (IBM, n=6): safe; 2/6 improved on 6MWT. Kota 2009 (AAV8-FS315 mouse): muscle mass +73%, specific force +12%.
Translational Gaps: Systemic delivery for whole-body effect; long-term reproductive/endocrine effects of activin blockade; phase III efficacy trials pending; dose–response in healthy muscle vs dystrophic; potential bone density effects.
Key References (DOIs): Haidet Proc Natl Acad Sci 2009 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0709144104 | Mendell Mol Ther 2015 https://doi.org/10.1038/mt.2015.36 | Mendell Neurology 2017 https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000004485
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Follistatin is NOT myostatin-specific — it also neutralises activins (reproductive hormones) and GDF-11 (disputed aging factor). Long-term endocrine consequences unknown. FST-344 includes a heparin-binding domain that limits systemic distribution vs FST-315; this is a feature for local injection but limits whole-body effects. Becker MD patients had heterogeneous baseline function. IBM is notoriously hard to treat — modest benefit is still notable. COMMERCIAL AVAILABILITY: As of 2025, follistatin plasmid therapy is offered at clinics in Honduras (Prospera ZEDE), Bahamas, and Panama through Minicircle (https://minicircle.io/) at ~$25,000/treatment, and through Unlimited Bio (https://unlimited.bio/) using similar plasmid delivery. These are non-integrating plasmid therapies (not AAV as in the Mendell published trials) with effects lasting ~1 year; no peer-reviewed human efficacy data has been published by these providers. Company-reported biomarker improvements (epigenetic age reduction, muscle mass gains) have not been independently verified.

Narrative: The Greenland shark thrives in icy, oxygen-variable Arctic waters for centuries. FTH1B encodes an expanded ferritin heavy chain that sequesters free iron with exceptional efficiency, preventing Fenton chemistry-driven oxidative damage. This molecular iron vault may be a core longevity mechanism, neutralizing one of the most destructive sources of cellular damage before it begins.
Short Description: An iron-storage protein locks loose iron inside a cage, stopping it from generating hydroxyl radicals that shred cell membranes. Greenland sharks carry extra gene copies and show the lowest labile iron and lipid damage of any elasmobranch, with copy number tracking maximum lifespan across the group. This exists only in shark tissue: no mammalian trial, no clinic, no product. Lock iron up too well and cells starve for it, causing functional deficiency despite normal blood iron.
Mechanism: FTH1B ferroxidase activity converts Fe2+ to Fe3+ for safe storage within the ferritin cage. The shark variant shows expanded copy number and enhanced iron-binding capacity, dramatically reducing labile iron pool and preventing hydroxyl radical generation via Fenton reactions.
Achievements (effect sizes): Greenland shark tissues show extremely low labile iron and lipid peroxidation markers. FTH1B copy number expansion correlates with maximum lifespan across elasmobranch species.
Translational Gaps: Iron homeostasis is delicately balanced; excessive sequestration may cause functional iron deficiency. Cross-species expression studies in mammalian models are needed.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaj2220
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Part of a multi-gene iron management system; isolated overexpression may not recapitulate full benefit.

Narrative: The Antarctic yeast Glaciozyma antarctica survives permanently frozen sea ice by producing a powerful antifreeze protein (AFP). GaAFP is a 26.6 kDa ice-binding protein that inhibits ice recrystallization — preventing the growth of large, tissue-destroying ice crystals. Unlike fish AFPs that primarily lower freezing point, GaAFP excels at ice recrystallization inhibition, the property most relevant to organ and cell cryopreservation.
Short Description: This protein coats forming ice crystals with a flat binding face, blocking them from fusing into the large shards that shred cells during freezing. In frozen vegetable trials it cut drip loss by 40-60% and boosted post-thaw cell survival. It's produced at high yield in Pichia pastoris yeast for food use, but organ and tissue cryopreservation in humans has never been tested. No food-grade regulatory approval exists yet, so it isn't sold or used clinically anywhere today.
Mechanism: GaAFP binds to ice crystal surfaces through a flat ice-binding face, inhibiting crystal growth and recrystallization. It functions primarily through ice recrystallization inhibition (IRI) rather than thermal hysteresis, making it particularly effective for protecting cells and tissues during freeze-thaw cycles at concentrations where thermal hysteresis AFPs are insufficient.
Achievements (effect sizes): Recombinant GaAFP reduces drip loss in frozen vegetables by 40-60%. GaAFP-treated frozen cells show significantly higher post-thaw viability. Protein expressed at high yields in Pichia pastoris.
Translational Gaps: Food-grade regulatory approval for AFP additives. Scaling Pichia pastoris production to industrial volumes. Demonstrating benefit for clinical cryopreservation of organs and tissues.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Complements existing AFP gene (fish AFP/AFGP) in the library with a distinct mechanism (IRI vs thermal hysteresis).

Narrative: Green fluorescent protein was isolated from crystal jellyfish in 1962 by Osamu Shimomura, cloned in 1992, demonstrated as a reporter gene by Martin Chalfie in 1994, and used to light up creatures from E. coli to marmosets. It won the 2008 Nobel Prize and rewrote experimental biology — you can now watch a specific gene turn on, a single protein move, or a tumor grow, just by attaching GFP and shining blue light. The protein needs no substrate, no cofactor, nothing except oxygen to fold itself into its own chromophore. There are fluorescent pigs, rabbits, mice, zebrafish, monkeys, and at least one glow-in-the-dark cat. The honest caveat is that GFP is emphatically a laboratory reporter, not a therapeutic. Its green emission barely penetrates tissue; it's mildly immunogenic in humans, which is why adoptive cell therapies quietly dropped it. Human clinical imaging long ago moved to PET tracers that see through the whole body.
Short Description: Cells carrying this protein glow green under blue light, folding the colour into their own barrel-shaped chromophore using nothing but oxygen. It has been put into everything from E. coli to transgenic marmosets with germline transmission. No clinic uses it in people, because green light barely escapes a few millimetres of tissue and PET reporters took its job. It is also mildly immunogenic, so cell therapies quietly dropped it.
Mechanism: 238-aa 11-β-strand barrel; autocatalytic S65-Y66-G67 chromophore; requires only O2 (no cofactor/substrate).
Achievements (effect sizes): Universal reporter across E. coli, yeast, plants, C. elegans, Drosophila (Chalfie 1994 Science); zebrafish; Tg mice (Okabe 1997 "green mice" CAG-EGFP ubiquitous); Tg pigs (Hwang/Lai 2006); Tg marmoset with germline transmission (Sasaki 2009 Nature); Tg cats (Wongsrikeao 2011 Nat Methods, co-expressed with TRIMCyp, FIV-resistant); routine in every human cell line. EGFP ε~56,000 M−1cm−1, QY 0.6, single-cell detection. c3GFP photostable mutant (2020) permits STED super-resolution.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (human cells routinely); T5 across multiple mammalian species; T7 ex-vivo only (not approved in vivo in humans)
Translational Gaps: Clinical in-vivo reporter role ceded to HSV1-TK ([18F]FHBG PET), NIS, PSMA, eDHFR/DYR-TMP.
Key References (DOIs): Chalfie Science 1994 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.8303295 | Okabe FEBS Lett 1997 https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-5793(97)00313-X | Sasaki Nature 2009 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08090
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Reporter, not enhancement; green emission doesn't penetrate tissue; O2-dependent maturation; photobleaching; mildly immunogenic in humans — cleared from adoptive-cell therapies. Human clinical imaging uses PET reporters, not GFP.

Narrative: The Venus' flower basket sponge (Euplectella aspergillum) builds an intricate glass skeleton at ambient temperature and pressure — a feat human engineering cannot match. Glassin is the silica-precipitating protein that templates this process, directing dissolved silicic acid into precisely organized nanoscale glass fibers with fiber-optic-grade optical clarity. This biological glass factory operates where industrial synthesis requires extreme heat.
Short Description: This protein folds silicic acid into glass fibers inside a living body, at room temperature and neutral pH, no furnace needed. Sponge spicules made this way transmit light like fiber-optic cable but flex more without snapping. So far this only works in Euplectella aspergillum, the Venus flower basket sponge, and lab dishes of recombinant protein — no human use exists. The catch: full skeleton strength needs several sponge proteins together, and glassin alone is unproven for bone implants.
Mechanism: Glassin contains a unique silica-condensing domain that catalyzes polycondensation of silicic acid. The protein self-assembles into filaments that template hierarchical silica deposition, creating structures with superior mechanical properties to synthetic glass fibers — combining strength, flexibility, and optical waveguide capability.
Achievements (effect sizes): Recombinant glassin produces amorphous silica nanoparticles at room temperature and neutral pH. Sponge spicules show fiber-optic light transmission with better flexibility than industrial optical fibers.
Translational Gaps: Scaling recombinant production for industrial application. Multi-protein cooperation in vivo may be required for full structural hierarchy. Biocompatibility for medical implants needs validation.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Most advanced bio-glass material known. Potential applications in optical sensors, bone scaffolds, and room-temperature glass manufacturing.

Narrative: The naked mole-rat is virtually immune to cancer and lives 10x longer than similar-sized rodents. Its fructose metabolism pathway is uniquely altered — GLUT5 transporter and ketohexokinase (KHK) show reduced expression, effectively blocking fructose-driven lipogenesis and metabolic syndrome. This natural metabolic rewiring may explain the species' remarkable resistance to obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disease.
Short Description: The gut absorbs less fructose and the liver cannot turn it into fat, blocking the sugar rush that drives obesity and diabetes. Naked mole-rats run this way naturally and stay metabolically healthy across a 31-year lifespan. Pfizer's KHK-blocking drug PF-06835919 already reached Phase 2 for fatty liver disease, after cutting liver fat 80% in mice. Dialling KHK down too far risks the same buildup seen in inherited fructose intolerance.
Mechanism: Downregulated GLUT5 limits cellular fructose uptake. Reduced KHK activity prevents fructose phosphorylation and subsequent de novo lipogenesis, uric acid production, and ATP depletion. Together they block the fructose-driven metabolic syndrome cascade.
Achievements (effect sizes): Naked mole-rats show no age-related metabolic decline. KHK inhibitors in mice reduce hepatic steatosis by 80%. Pfizer KHK inhibitor PF-06835919 reached Phase 2 clinical trials for NASH.
Translational Gaps: Species-specific metabolic context may limit direct translation. KHK inhibition in humans needs careful monitoring for hereditary fructose intolerance-like effects.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: KHK pharmaceutical inhibitors already in clinical development independently of NMR biology.

Narrative: Greenland sharks swim through Arctic depths for 272 to 392 years — some individuals were alive before the American Revolution. Julius Nielsen dated them by radiocarbon-dating their eye lenses in 2016, making them the longest-lived vertebrates known. In 2024, a preprint from Alessandro Cellerino's group reported a 6.45-Gb genome assembly: 81 duplicated genes enriched for DNA double-strand-break repair, three copies of RAD51, expanded NF-κB signaling, and a unique lysine insertion in the C-terminus of p53 that AlphaFold predicts would extend an alpha-helix. All of it, so far, is comparative genomics — no one has expressed the shark p53 variant in a cell, knocked it into a mouse, or done any functional assay whatsoever. The shark is essentially unculturable; you cannot easily get primary cells. It's the most tantalizing longevity genome we have, and simultaneously the one furthest from any experiment a lab could actually run next Tuesday.
Short Description: Cells get their DNA cut by breaks, and this network patches them before they turn into mutations or cell death. Greenland sharks carry 81 duplicated repair genes, three copies of RAD51, and a lysine insertion in p53, and one shark aged this way was at least 272 years old. It's a 2024 preprint only — no lab has expressed the shark p53 variant in a cell or mouse, since the species can't be cultured. The catch: extra RAD51 drives cancer in mammals instead of preventing it.
Mechanism: 81 duplicated genes forming DSB-repair GO-enriched STRING network; RAD51 in 3 copies (one intronless retrotranspositional); NF2 duplication; unique lysine insertion in p53 HKKEKE C-terminal motif predicted (AlphaFold3) to extend helix.
Achievements (effect sizes): Sahm 2024 bioRxiv (preprint): 6.45 Gb chromosome-level assembly; 22,634 genes; statistical enrichment p=0.029 (network), FDR=0.002 with TP53. Nielsen 2016 Science: lens radiocarbon dating → minimum ages 272 y. Nothing else — all predictions purely computational; no functional assay on GLS p53 variant; no mouse knock-in; no heterologous cell test; no tissue culture possible.
Translational Gaps: Everything — expression/functional validation of GLS p53 variant; knock-in mouse; cell models.
Key References (DOIs): Sahm bioRxiv 2024 https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.09.09.611499 | Nielsen Science 2016 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Preprint; no expression/functional validation; p53 CTD structural prediction is low-confidence; RAD51 overexpression is oncogenic in mammals. "512-yr shark" = upper 95.4% CI bound; measured floor is ~272 y.

Narrative: The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) lives over 400 years — the longest-lived vertebrate known. H1F0 encodes histone H1.0, a linker histone that stabilizes chromatin architecture.
